summary: Specifies T/TCP, an experimental extension that lets TCP handle short request and response exchanges efficiently. It is historic. It was replaced by RFC 6247.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally, two computers have a long hello before talking. This shortcut lets quick questions go faster. It was later retired.

subtitle: TCP extensions to speed up request-response exchanges without a slow handshake.

tldr.problem: TCP was designed for streaming data, not request-response interactions. The three-way handshake and TIME-WAIT delays add latency to transaction-oriented applications.
tldr.mechanism: T/TCP introduces connection counts to bypass the handshake and shorten connection cleanup, allowing rapid request-response exchanges with minimal packet overhead.
tldr.outcome: T/TCP became historic and was superseded; request-response performance is better served by other mechanisms today.

today: RFC 1644 is Historic. It has been obsoleted by RFC 6247. T/TCP was experimental and never achieved wide deployment. Modern approaches to reducing transaction latency in TCP have superseded it.

sections.title: Request-Response Over TCP
sections.content:
TCP was designed as a virtual circuit protocol for streaming data. It assumes long-lived connections where the overhead of opening and closing is small compared to the time spent transferring data. However, many applications use TCP for request-response interactions where a client sends a request and waits for a response before closing the connection. Examples include DNS queries, SNMP requests, and HTTP transactions.

In request-response mode, TCP imposes two performance problems. First, the three-way handshake adds an extra round-trip time before any application data can be sent. Second, closing the connection leaves the TCP endpoint in TIME-WAIT state for 2 times the maximum segment lifetime, typically 240 seconds. This prevents rapid successive transactions using the same port pair.

T/TCP is an experimental TCP extension that addresses these issues. It remains backward-compatible with standard TCP and uses a new connection count mechanism to validate that SYN segments are not replayed and to safely truncate TIME-WAIT state.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP takes time to connect and disconnect, which matters when you are just asking a quick question. T/TCP skips some steps to make it faster, while keeping it safe from old packets arriving late.

sections.title: How T/TCP Works
sections.content:
T/TCP introduces a 32-bit connection count field that increments with each new connection from a host. The server caches the most recent connection count from each client. When a new SYN segment arrives, the server compares its connection count against the cached value using modular arithmetic.

If the new connection count is larger than the cached value, the TCP Accelerated Open mechanism allows the server to accept the SYN and begin processing data immediately without waiting for the three-way handshake. This is safe because the monotonically increasing connection count guarantees the SYN cannot be an old duplicate from an earlier connection.

For connections shorter than the maximum segment lifetime, T/TCP can truncate TIME-WAIT state because the connection count is unique to that incarnation. When the client initiates a new transaction using the same port, its SYN implicitly acknowledges the previous connection and starts fresh. This allows high-rate transaction processing without exhausting port space or kernel state.

Three new TCP options carry connection counts: the CC option carries the current count, CC.NEW is sent after a client restart or wraparound to invalidate the server cache, and CC.ECHO echoes the client's count back to validate the SYN,ACK response.
sections.plainLanguage: Every connection gets a number. The server remembers the biggest number it saw from each client. When a new connection arrives with a bigger number, the server knows it is not an old copy of a past connection, so it can skip the handshake. When you are done, you can start a new connection right away because the number proves it is new.

sections.title: Connection States and Sequences
sections.content:
T/TCP extends TCP's state machine with starred states that indicate the connection is half-synchronized. When the TAO test succeeds, the ESTABLISHED and LISTEN states become ESTABLISHED* and LISTEN, indicating that a SYN still needs to be sent or acknowledged.

A minimal T/TCP transaction takes three segments and one round-trip time. The client sends a SYN with request data and a connection count. The server immediately accepts the data, generates a response, and sends a SYN,ACK with the response data and echoed connection count. The client acknowledges the SYN,ACK. If either endpoint needs to send more data, the connection transitions to normal TCP operation.

T/TCP applications must decide whether to use fixed or varying port pairs. For high-frequency transactions to the same server, reusing the same local port allows time-wait truncation and gets full T/TCP performance. For lower-frequency transactions or diverse destinations, using different local ports is acceptable.

Special rules handle edge cases: client crashes that reset the connection count, wraparound of the 32-bit counter, and overlapping old and new connection states. Connection states for incoming SYNs during TIME-WAIT use intermediate I-states to bridge the old and new incarnations.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection has special states that mean we are partway done with the handshake. A quick transaction is three packets: request, response, and acknowledgment. If there is more to say, it becomes a normal TCP connection.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must maintain a per-host cache of the most recent connection count and optionally other values like round-trip time, congestion window, and maximum segment size. The cache is consulted only when establishing connections, allowing safe reuse of cache entries during a connection's lifetime without locking.

Proper round-trip time measurement is more complex for transactions than for streaming. A single transaction provides one RTT sample, so implementations should cache RTT estimates across transactions. The cached value must be a weighted average of previous estimates, with suitable time constants chosen for transactional traffic rather than file transfer.

Processing a minimal T/TCP transaction without the delays in a normal three-way handshake requires careful handling of data in the initial SYN segment. The implementation must queue the SYN data until the connection is validated, then deliver it to the application immediately after the TAO test succeeds.

The connection count generator must ensure monotonicity across restarts. The specification requires that counts do not advance faster than 2 to the 31st counts per 2 times the maximum segment lifetime. This allows millions of transactions per second even with liberal maximum segment lifetime assumptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The server must remember a number for each client and look it up quickly. Measuring how fast the network is becomes important for guessing how long to wait for responses. The implementation must be careful to handle data that arrives in the first packet, before the connection is fully set up.
